source: Liu, Padmanabhan & Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems
finding: A NeurIPS 2026 FAST workshop position paper that brings Kirsh and Maglio's idea to LLM agents. It splits epistemic action into three modes: acquiring missing evidence, transforming evidence that is hard to use, and probing a system to create a revealing response.
numbers: Three modes (acquisitive, transformative, probing). No experiments and no measured results; it is an argument paper.
quote: Cognitive science calls actions that improve the basis for a later choice epistemic actions.
limits: Position paper only. It says no existing system chooses among all three modes and justifies both acting and stopping. It tests nothing itself.
agent_relevance: Gives a clean vocabulary for S4: code probes are probing actions, reformatting data is transformative, asking the user is acquisitive.

source: Liu, Padmanabhan & Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems
finding: Writes the choice of epistemic action as value-of-information: pick the action e that maximises expected value of the later decision minus the cost of e, with commit-now as the null action. The scaffold fixes the action set, so a perfect value estimate cannot pick an action the scaffold omits.
numbers: Formula: e* = argmax over E plus null of (E[V(I_e)|I,e] - c(e)); null action has cost 0.
limits: The paper says how an agent estimates this value and validates it is still an open problem.
agent_relevance: Argues for a scaffold that lists probe types explicitly (run code, perturb one input, compare two cases) rather than hoping the model invents them.

source: Liu, Padmanabhan & Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems
finding: Proposes a minimal benchmark for epistemic competence: hold task, model, prompt budget and pragmatic actions fixed, and vary whether acquisition, transformation and probing are available. Separately test (1) noticing the evidence is inadequate, (2) choosing an action, (3) using the result. Compare action given explicitly with action available but not suggested.
numbers: Proposed design only; no numbers.
limits: Not yet run by anyone as far as this search found.
agent_relevance: Gives an ablation recipe for our agent: probe tool available vs probe prescribed vs no probe tool.

source: Liu, Padmanabhan & Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems
finding: Says auditable traces must record the pending decision, the evidence before and after the action, and the expected evidential change; a bare tool call does not show purpose. It also warns that transformations can discard information and probes can introduce artefacts.
numbers: Not quantitative.
limits: Position claim, untested.
agent_relevance: Suggests logging for every probe: what decision is pending, what the agent expects to learn, and what it learned. Fits a probe record in S4.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang & Slivkins (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Tested GPT-3.5, GPT-4 and Llama-2 as agents in multi-armed bandits with many prompt designs. Only one configuration explored well: GPT-4 with chain of thought and an external summary of the history as sufficient statistics. All others failed to explore robustly.
numbers: 1 configuration succeeded out of all tested. GPT-4 with the basic prompt had a suffix failure (never picks the best arm again after some round) in more than 60% of replicates.
quote: only one configuration resulted in satisfactory exploratory behavior
limits: Simple bandits, 2023-era models. Newer reasoning models not tested here. Exploration here is choosing arms, not probing with code.
agent_relevance: Models under-explore on their own. Our S4 probe step likely needs to be forced by the scaffold and the history summarised, not left to free choice.

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Underspecified tasks where exactly one missing variable blocks the answer; the model must pick the one right clarifying question from options. Models do well on math (GSM-Q, GSME-Q) but score only about 40-50% or lower on logic (Logic-Q) and planning (Planning-Q).
numbers: GSME-Q over 80%, GSM-Q mostly 85-99% for strong models; Logic-Q and Planning-Q under 50% (many cells 25-40%). Models: GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 Sonnet, Gemini 1.5/2.0, Gemma 2.
quote: models struggle to identify the right question even when they can solve the fully specified version
limits: Multiple choice of questions, not open-ended probing. Single missing variable only. Models of 2024-25.
agent_relevance: Knowing which probe to run is a separate skill from solving the problem. Do not assume a model that solves the task will pick the right probe.

source: Li, Kim & Wang (2025) QuestBench: Can LLMs ask the right question to acquire information in reasoning tasks?
finding: Question accuracy was checked against problem complexity, and the paper finds being able to solve the fully specified problem is not enough. Filtering to problems the model can solve moved question accuracy up by as much as 39% for some models and down about 10% for others.
numbers: Change after filtering to solvable problems: up to +39 points for some models, about -10 for others. Spearman correlations were reported against complexity axes (values not copied here).
limits: Effects mixed by model; neither Logic-Q nor Planning-Q reached 100% after filtering.
agent_relevance: Reasoning ability and probe-choosing ability come apart, so the scaffold should score probes on their own.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: UoT simulates possible futures, scores each candidate question by expected information gain, and picks the best. Across 20 Questions, medical diagnosis and troubleshooting it raised task success by an average of 38.1% over direct prompting and cut the number of questions needed.
numbers: Average +38.1% success over direct prompting across five datasets and several LLMs; +46.6% for Llama3-70B. Llama3-70B closed-set: 20Q Common 51.4 to 55.9, MedDG 83.7 to 90.4, FloDial 28.8 to 47.1; mean conversation length in successes on MedDG fell from 3.5 to 1.0. Up to 97.0% on DX with GPT-4.
limits: Baseline is plain direct prompting; the gain over the strongest baseline (adapted tree of thoughts) is much smaller. Answers come from a simulated patient or oracle.
agent_relevance: A structured which-question-is-most-informative step beats free asking. Supports an explicit information-gain choice in S4 instead of a bare probe-first rule.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Uncertainty of Thoughts: Uncertainty-Aware Planning Enhances Information Seeking in LLMs
finding: Ablations show the uncertainty-based reward and the reward propagation each matter, and that simulating deeper futures helps up to a point. A pruned version cuts cost.
numbers: Pruned UoT beat Adapted-ToT by 7.36% in the text; UoT beat CoT-SC by 33.8% on average; depth experiments in Appendix E.
limits: Cost is higher than direct prompting; tree search over questions needs many model calls.
agent_relevance: Information-gain scoring costs tokens; apply it only where a wrong first attempt is expensive.

source: Choudhury et al. (2026) BED-LLM: Intelligent Information Gathering with LLMs and Bayesian Experimental Design
finding: Chooses each next question by maximising expected information gain, estimated from the LLM's own predictive distributions. On 20 Questions it raised success by 37.4 percentage points on average over direct prompting, more than doubling success in over half the setups and never lowering it.
numbers: +37.4 percentage points average success vs Prompt-Only (ICLR 2026). Ablations: Entropy was the strongest alternative; a proper non-deterministic likelihood mattered for targeting real EIG; Implicit Maximisation (prompt the model to pick the most informative of the candidate questions) beat Prompt-Only cheaply.
limits: 20 Questions and movie preference elicitation; answerers are simulated LLMs. Extra compute for EIG estimation.
agent_relevance: Even a cheap prompt variant (pick the most informative among candidates) helped; full EIG helped most. Candidate-then-select is a usable S4 pattern.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu & van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: Frames clarifying questions as Bayesian experimental design over the space of possible solutions instead of the space of questions. Reasoning directly about solutions (EIG-uniform) beat implicit question choice and implicit tree-of-thought choice in 20 Questions and code generation.
numbers: 20 Questions: average rank over 15 target animals, 5 run seeds, 25 evaluation seeds; EIG-uniform ranked best at every step (e.g. 4.1 at step 10 vs 6.2 for the worst strategy in one model). Also HumanEval and APPS (48 and 47 tasks after filtering).
limits: Rank scores, not raw success; GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4o-mini. EIG-logprobs did worse than EIG-uniform.
agent_relevance: Probe choice should come from thinking about what answers remain possible, not from asking what is a good question. Matches enumerate hypotheses, then pick the probe that splits them.

source: Kobalczyk, Astorga, Liu & van der Schaar (2025) Active Task Disambiguation with LLMs
finding: The authors argue that good question asking needs a form of meta-cognitive reasoning that LLMs may lack, and shift the load from implicit to explicit reasoning about the space of viable solutions.
numbers: Qualitative claim backed by the rankings in the 20 Questions and code-generation experiments.
limits: Argument is partly interpretive.
agent_relevance: Supports an explicit list-the-remaining-possibilities sub-step before choosing any probe.

source: Wu (2023) Large Language Models Should Ask Clarifying Questions to Increase Confidence in Generated Code
finding: A short exploratory paper arguing code LLMs should ask clarifying and probing questions before generating final code, using an LLM-generated communicator to find ambiguity or low confidence.
numbers: No measured results reported; the paper presents a process and calls itself an initial step.
limits: Vision paper with no benchmark numbers. Treat as a pointer, not evidence of effect.
agent_relevance: Shows the idea is circulating but unproven; do not cite as support for a gain.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou & Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Across 200,000+ simulated conversations, all top models did worse when information arrived across turns than when given in one instruction. Models guessed early, produced a final answer too soon, and then leaned on that answer.
numbers: Average drop of 39% across six generation tasks; aptitude down about 15%, unreliability up about 112%.
quote: LLMs often make assumptions in early turns and prematurely attempt to generate final solutions
limits: Simulated users with sharded instructions. The cause named is premature answer attempts, not lack of questions as such.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence for the failure S4 targets: committing to a full attempt before the missing facts are in. A rule of no full attempt until the probe is back addresses it.

source: Laban, Hayashi, Zhou & Neville (2025) LLMs Get Lost in Multi-Turn Conversation
finding: Setups include CONCAT (all shards in one turn) as a check that rephrasing alone does not cause the drop; a model that does well on CONCAT but badly on SHARDED struggles specifically with multi-turn underspecification.
numbers: Conditions: full, concat, sharded, recap, snowball; sharded is the underspecified multi-turn case.
limits: Simulated user, not real users.
agent_relevance: Gives a ready test design to measure whether a probe-first gate recovers the single-turn score.

source: Matsnev (2026) Uncertainty Decomposition for Clarification Seeking in LLM Agents
finding: A prompt-only method separates action confidence from request uncertainty so an agent asks for clarification when the task is ambiguous. Tested on WebShop-Clarification and ALFWorld-Clarification where 50% of tasks are made underspecified, across five backbones.
numbers: Clarification F1 on ALFWorld-Clarification up 73% over ReAct+UE and 36% over UAM on average; best on all five backbones on WebShop-Clarification and four of five on ALFWorld-Clarification. Backbones: GPT-5.1, DeepSeek-v3.2-exp, GLM-4.7, Qwen3.5-35B, GPT-OSS-120B.
limits: Measures F1 of deciding to ask, not final task success in the abstract; the ambiguity is injected by the authors.
agent_relevance: A cheap prompt: keep am-I-sure-of-the-action separate from is-the-request-clear. Could be a gate before S4 asks or probes.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration?
finding: Blicket-style nexiom detector task. Human adults who chose their own tests learned conjunctive rules much better than passive observers; LLMs with the same action space did not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions and explored less efficiently.
numbers: Human study 102 participants, active vs passive observation (yoked) plus a supplementary Passive Proposer group. LLMs: gpt-5, gpt-5-mini, o4-mini, gemini-2.5-flash, deepseek-reasoner, deepseek-chat; 288 LLM trials. gpt-5 and deepseek-reasoner near-perfect on disjunctive rules; conjunctive harder for all. 16% of average humans got both rule and objects wrong in conjunctive.
quote: LLMs do not consistently gain from choosing their own interventions
limits: Preprint; small task with 4 objects. Exact LLM-vs-human percentages sit in figures I did not transcribe.
agent_relevance: A close modern test of whether acting to learn helps: the benefit humans get from active testing is not automatic for models. Probing must be designed, not just allowed.

source: Samiei et al. (2026) Human Adults and LLMs as Scientists: Who Benefits from Active Exploration?
finding: Stronger reasoning models such as gpt-5 adjust the number of objects per test to the remaining uncertainty, like better human explorers. Weaker models explored less efficiently.
numbers: Information gain measured as log2 of hypotheses remaining; humans needed about 9.6 tests for conjunctive vs 6.4 for disjunctive (Table 2 text).
limits: Read from text; figure details not checked.
agent_relevance: Efficiency of probing differs by model strength. Cheaper models may need a stricter probe protocol (change one thing at a time, keep a hypothesis list).

source: Guo et al. (2026) SWE-Doctor: Guiding Software Engineering Agents with Runtime Diagnosis from Multi-Faceted Bug Reproduction Tests
finding: A preliminary study found that handing an agent a generated bug-reproduction test does not improve patch generation: fail-to-pass tests cover one manifestation of the bug, fail-to-fail tests mislead. SWE-Doctor instead runs several reproduction tests and uses the runtime diagnosis (the probe result) to guide the patch.
numbers: SWE-Doctor 75.7% on SWE-bench Verified and 59.4% on SWE-bench Pro (averages over 5 LLM backends); +2.0 and +3.9 points over mini-SWE-agent and live-SWE-agent on Verified; +8.0 to 8.9 points on Pro. Backends: GPT-5.4, GPT-5.4-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.6, DeepSeek-V4-Pro, MiMo-V2.5-Pro. Uniquely resolves more than twice as many issues as either baseline.
limits: A single probe did not help; the gain came from multi-faceted probes plus diagnosis. Authors' own method, not independently replicated.
agent_relevance: Direct code-probe evidence for S4: a probe helps only if it reveals the right part of the problem; one narrow probe can anchor the agent on a partial fix. Use several probes and read the runtime result.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Scaling Test-Time Compute for Agentic Coding
finding: Only the abstract and first page were read. Turns long agent trajectories into compact summaries of hypotheses, progress and failure modes, then votes or conditions new rollouts on them.
numbers: Claude-4.5-Opus 70.9% to 77.6% on SWE-Bench Verified (mini-SWE-agent); 46.9% to 59.1% on Terminal-Bench v2.0.
limits: Full paper not read in detail; the gain is from summarising whole attempts, not from probing as such.
agent_relevance: A transformative epistemic action (compress to the useful structure) improves later decisions; the Krishnamurthy result also needed summarised history.

source: Wang (2026) Same Pieces, Different Servers: A Tetris Benchmark for AI Agents as Served
finding: A 2026 Tetris benchmark for language-model agents scores every move against an oracle and a beam-search bot. It is about serving cost and latency, not epistemic (rotate-to-see) actions. Each option is a precomputed placement with its simulated outcome, so the agent never needs to rotate a piece to see how it fits.
numbers: Nine open-weight models, five pre-specified experiments, 100 pieces per game; gemma-4-31B scored 76 vs the Intelif decision model 54; resending history costs little with cached input but would cost 11-12 times more if not cached and makes play worse.
limits: Gap note: options are pre-simulated, which removes the very thing Kirsh and Maglio studied. It cannot test epistemic rotation.
agent_relevance: No LLM Tetris test of the epistemic-action hypothesis was found; a test would hide the placement result and let the agent rotate or simulate first.

source: Search record (this run, 2026-11-01): arXiv and OpenAlex queries for LLM tests of Kirsh and Maglio's Tetris hypothesis
finding: Found no experiment that gives an LLM the rotate-to-see choice from Tetris and measures epistemic versus pragmatic moves. The only LLM paper naming epistemic action as a design concept is the position paper (c01). Applied work (clarifying questions, bug-reproduction tests, EIG question choice) uses the idea without the name.
numbers: Queries returned the 2026 position paper and the Tetris serving benchmark only.
limits: Absence in a few capped searches, not proof of absence.
agent_relevance: Our agent cannot lean on a direct LLM replication; lean on the neighbouring question-asking and bug-reproduction results.

source: Liu, Padmanabhan & Viswanathan (2026) Before Agents Decide: Epistemic Action in LLM-Based Systems
finding: The paper's examples of probing in agent benchmarks: ScienceWorld (build a circuit to find conductivity), DiscoveryWorld (form hypotheses, run experiments), and a bias-audit system that generates matched image pairs to create a contrast absent from the data.
numbers: Examples only, no scores quoted.
limits: The paper cites these as capabilities and reports no results for them.
agent_relevance: Candidate environments for testing our probe step: ScienceWorld and DiscoveryWorld.

source: Krishnamurthy, Harris, Foster, Zhang & Slivkins (2024) Can Large Language Models Explore In-Context?
finding: Besides suffix failures, a second failure mode is uniform behaviour: choosing all arms about equally often and never narrowing down. The authors suggest fine-tuning or dataset curation may be needed for harder settings.
numbers: Plotted suffix-failure frequency against uniform-like failure per model and prompt pair at T=100; only one point (GPT-4 with summarised history and CoT) is good on both.
limits: Bandit setting and 2023 models.
agent_relevance: Warns that explore-more prompts can produce aimless probing as well as too little; probes need a stated purpose.

source: Yao et al. (2023) ReAct: Synergizing Reasoning and Acting in Language Models
finding: Interleaves thought with tool actions such as search so observations inform later reasoning. Cited by the position paper as acquisitive epistemic action. Not opened in this run.
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Unverified in this run; pointer only.
agent_relevance: The basic loop S4 builds on: act to get an observation, then reason.

source: Yang et al. (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces Enable Automated Software Engineering
finding: Shows interface design changes agent success on software tasks. The position paper uses it as an example of transformative scaffolding. Not opened in this run.
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Unverified in this run; pointer only.
agent_relevance: Interface shape decides which probes are cheap; make probes cheap in our scaffold.

source: Xia et al. (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed pipeline of localise, repair and test selection, including reproduction tests, with no free agent loop. Not opened in this run (another evidence file in this folder covers it).
numbers: Not verified here.
limits: Unverified in this run; pointer only.
agent_relevance: A scripted probe step (reproduce first) can compete with open-ended agents.
